screens.title: Fetching Data with URLSession
screens.narratorSegment: Networking is what lets your app become data-driven. In iOS the foundational A P I for HTTP work is URLSession. In this lesson you will learn how to form valid URLs, wrap them when needed in URLRequest, and use URLSession. shared. dataTask to perform GET requests. We will emphasize safe patterns: checking for network errors first, verifying HTTP status codes, and decoding data. You will also learn why App Transport Security forces HTTPS by default and how that shapes secure A P I choices. A compact Swift example will show a real GET request against a public test endpoint, and a small SwiftUI activity later will connect that fetch to a list of posts. By the end you will understand the standard completion-handler pattern and how to avoid common mistakes like blocking the main thread or assuming data is always present. Keep an eye on status codes, treat the completion handler as asynchronous, and plan to move decoding to the next step. Consider how your app should behave when the network is slow — what feedback will you show the user?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Fetching Data with URLSession
Fetching Data with URLSession
Make simple GET requests to retrieve remote data safely
In this lesson

Understand URL, URLRequest, and URLSession; run a GET request; handle the completion handler; and respect App Transport Security.

Why it matters

Networked apps can serve fresh content, sync user data, and integrate with cloud services. Robust networking avoids crashes and keeps the UI responsive.

Coming up

Hands-on Swift examples and a small SwiftUI fetcher show how to wire requests to visible UI lists without blocking the main thread.

Explore Key Topics
URL & URLRequest
Define where and how to call an API; URLRequest adds headers and method control.
URLSession.dataTask
Performs the GET request asynchronously and returns data, response, and error via a completion handler.
ATS & Security
iOS requires secure HTTPS by default; use TLS endpoints to avoid ATS problems.
Concept map
How a GET request flows
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
URL
URLRequest
URLSession
Small arrows connect these cards conceptually: URL identifies the endpoint, URLRequest configures the method and headers, and URLSession performs the transfer and calls back with data, response, and error.

screens.title: What you'll learn — part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives frame the practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand networking fundamentals in iOS and why URLSession is the primary A P I for HTTP work. That concept includes recognizing when to use the shared session versus a custom session. Second, you'll learn how to construct valid URL and URLRequest objects so requests don't fail at runtime. We'll show how invalid URL strings lead to nil and how to guard against crashes. Third, you'll implement a basic GET request using URLSession. shared. dataTask, observe how the completion handler returns Data, URLResponse and Error, and learn the pattern of starting the task with resume(). Fourth, you will inspect responses safely by converting URLResponse to HTTPURLResponse and checking status codes before parsing data. Each objective is paired with a simple verification milestone so you can confirm competency in a tiny hands-on step.

keyIdea.title: Safety first
keyIdea.text: Always check for error, validate HTTP status codes, and move UI updates to the main queue. Prefer HTTPS to avoid ATS failures.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Learning Objectives
Practical checks
  • Check error first in the completion handler; a non-nil error means the network failed.
  • Cast response to HTTPURLResponse and validate statusCode in 200...299.
  • Only then unwrap and use Data to avoid nil crashes or meaningless parsing attempts.
Common mistake: assuming a non-nil data argument implies success. Always verify the status code as well.
UI and security patterns
  • Network tasks run asynchronously; do not block the main thread.
  • Dispatch UI updates via DispatchQueue.main.async when you update views.
  • Prefer HTTPS endpoints to avoid App Transport Security restrictions.
Mnemonic: network work off the main thread, UI work on the main thread.

screens.title: What is networking in iOS?
screens.narratorSegment: When we say "networking" in iOS, we mean the code path that lets an app send requests and receive responses over the internet. This includes everything from retrieving a JSON payload to downloading an image. URLSession is the native A P I that performs these tasks. Think of URLSession as the plumbing and worker threads: you hand it an address and instructions, it performs the transfer, and then it calls back with the results. A concrete example: an app fetches a list of posts to display in a feed. The app creates a URL pointing to the posts endpoint, calls URLSession. shared. dataTask, and when the server replies, the completion handler receives data or an error. A common misconception is that URLSession itself decodes responses into model objects. It does not; URLSession gives you raw Data. Decoding into Swift structs using JSONDecoder is a separate step. Another frequent confusion is assuming network calls are synchronous; they are asynchronous — you register a completion handler and resume the task. Key takeaway: URLSession executes HTTP work asynchronously and returns Data, response, and error; your job is to validate and decode safely.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is networking in iOS?
Definition

Networking is the process of sending requests to and receiving responses from external services. In iOS, URLSession performs requests and returns raw binary Data together with a response object and a possible network error.

Example
Fetching a list of posts from a remote API to populate a feed in your app.
Common mistake
Treating network calls as if they always return data. Always check error and status code first.
Pro tip
Prefer URLRequest when you need headers or methods other than GET; use the default URL for simple reads.
Visual explanation
A single request produces three pieces of information: a network-level error if the connection failed; a response object that can be cast to HTTPURLResponse for status code checking; and Data which holds the server payload. You must handle all three to be robust.
Key takeaway

URLSession returns raw data and response asynchronously; validating error → response → data avoids runtime issues.

screens.title: Constructing URLs and URLRequest
screens.narratorSegment: Building a valid URL and, when necessary, a URLRequest are small steps that prevent runtime errors. Start by creating a URL from a well-formed string. If URL(string:) returns nil, the string is invalid and you must handle that case before continuing. For simple GETs you can pass a URL directly to dataTask; for more control—adding headers, query parameters, or using other methods—wrap the URL in a URLRequest and set its httpMethod. A practical scenario: you want to request a protected resource and must include an Authorization header. You would build a URLRequest, set the header field, and then pass that request to dataTask. A common misconception is that adding percent-encoded query parameters is optional; incorrectly encoded URLs will fail to initialize. Also avoid force-unwrapping URL objects. In short: validate the string, safely construct URL, use URLRequest when you need configuration, and never rely on implicit unwrapping. This leads to more predictable error handling and easier debugging. Constructing URLs and URLRequest means validate url strings, prefer urlrequest when you need headers or methods, and avoid force-unwrapping to prevent runtime crashes.. In practical terms, make safe addresses and request objects for get operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Constructing URLs and URLRequest
Step-by-step
  1. 1. Validate the string: guard let url = URL(string: urlString) else { handle error }.
  2. 2. For simple GETs pass url directly to dataTask(with: url).
  3. 3. For headers or non-GET methods create var request = URLRequest(url: url) and set request.httpMethod and headers.
  4. 4. Start the task using resume() to perform the request.
Analogy
URL is the postal address. URLRequest is the envelope with a return address and postage — it carries extra instructions for delivery.
Common mistakes & examples
Forgetting to percent-encode query parameters can make URL(string:) return nil.
Use URLRequest to set headers like Authorization or Content-Type when needed.
Concrete example
// Creating a URL safely
let urlString = "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1"
guard let url = URL(string: urlString) else {
  print("Error: Invalid URL string provided.")
  return
}

// Optional: configure a request
var request = URLRequest(url: url)
request.httpMethod = "GET"
request.addValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Accept")
Remember: never force-unwrap URL(string:). Always guard against nil and report a meaningful error to aid debugging.

screens.title: Making a GET request with dataTask
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete GET-request function to solidify the pattern. The function begins by safely creating a URL. If that fails we print an error and return. Next we create a data task using URLSession. shared. dataTask(with: url) and provide a completion handler that receives data, response, and error. Inside the handler we first check error; a non-nil error typically indicates a connectivity or transport failure. If error is nil, we cast response to HTTPURLResponse and inspect the statusCode, accepting only codes in the 200 to 299 range. If the status code indicates a server-side problem we log it and return. Finally we check that data is non-nil and then convert it to a readable string for inspection. The final step is calling resume() on the task to start it. A common mistake is forgetting resume() or performing blocking work on the main thread. This pattern guarantees you see either an error, a non-success HTTP status, or readable data. Try running this function with a valid URL and an invalid URL to observe the different code paths. Making a GET request with dataTask means create the url, call datatask, check error → cast response and check status code → unwrap data → process. always call resume().. In practical terms, complete example: error, response, and data handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Making a GET request with dataTask
Complete Swift example
// Function to perform a GET request
func fetchPostData(from urlString: String) {
  guard let url = URL(string: urlString) else {
    print("Error: Invalid URL string provided.")
    return
  }

  let dataTask = URLSession.shared.dataTask(with: url) { (data, response, error) in
    // 1. Check for network-level errors
    if let error = error {
      print("Network error: \(error.localizedDescription)")
      return
    }

    // 2. Check for HTTP response status code
    guard let httpResponse = response as? HTTPURLResponse else {
      print("Error: Invalid response type.")
      return
    }

    guard (200...299).contains(httpResponse.statusCode) else {
      print("Server error: HTTP Status Code \(httpResponse.statusCode)")
      return
    }

    // 3. Check if data was received
    guard let data = data else {
      print("Error: No data received.")
      return
    }

    // 4. Process the data
    if let jsonString = String(data: data, encoding: .utf8) {
      print("Successfully fetched data:")
      print(jsonString)
    } else {
      print("Error: Could not decode data into UTF-8 string.")
    }
  }

  dataTask.resume()
}
This code demonstrates the typical flow: validate URL, create the task, perform ordered checks in the completion handler, and resume the task to start the request. Observing each check helps you decide how to surface errors to users or retry.
Example run
Call the function with a valid endpoint to print JSON as a string for inspection. Call it with an invalid host to observe network error output, and try an HTTP (non-HTTPS) address to see ATS behavior.
Misconception check
Do not assume data is valid just because it's non-nil. Always check HTTP status codes and handle server errors explicitly.
Key Takeaway

Follow the ordered checks and call resume() — that combination prevents many common networking bugs.

screens.title: URL vs URLRequest
screens.narratorSegment: Both URL and URLRequest appear in nearly every networked app. URL is simply the address of a resource. For basic GET requests where you only need to read a public endpoint, creating a URL and passing it directly to dataTask is concise and sufficient. URLRequest wraps a URL and provides configuration: the HTTP method, headers, timeout, and body. Use URLRequest when you must set an Authorization header, specify Content-Type, or switch to POST or PUT. A common beginner mistake is always wrapping with URLRequest even when unnecessary; that adds verbosity but doesn't harm functionality. Conversely, another mistake is trying to add headers by mutating a URL — headers belong to URLRequest. Example scenario: requesting a JSON feed without authentication — use URL directly. Example with authentication: build a URLRequest, set request. httpMethod = "GET", and add the Authorization header. Both are valid; choose the simpler option when possible and the configurable option when you need control. This keeps code readable and maintainable. URL vs URLRequest means use url for simple gets. use urlrequest when you need headers, custom methods, or other request configuration.. In practical terms, when to use the simple url and when to configure a request. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › URL vs URLRequest
URL (Simple)
Use when you only need to point to a public GET endpoint. Example: fetching a public post or an open JSON list. Pass the URL directly to dataTask(with: url) and call resume().
When to pick this
  • No headers required
  • Simple GET on a public endpoint
  • Concise and readable
URLRequest (Configurable)
Use when you need to set headers, a different HTTP method, a body, or timeout policies. Example: adding Authorization headers to call a protected API.
When to pick this
  • Custom headers like Authorization or Accept
  • Non-GET methods such as POST
  • When you need to set cache policy or timeout
Concrete example

Public feed: use URL. Protected resource: create URLRequest, set httpMethod and add headers, then pass the request to dataTask(with: request).

screens.title: Completion Handler Anatomy
screens.narratorSegment: The completion handler of dataTask delivers three optional values: Data?, URLResponse?, and Error?. These three items represent the result of the network operation. First, Error? indicates a network-level failure such as no internet, DNS lookup failure, or a cancelled request. If error is non-nil, you should usually stop and surface a friendly message. Second, URLResponse? holds metadata about the transfer and can often be cast to HTTPURLResponse to access the HTTP status code. That status code tells you whether the request was successful (200–299) or whether a client or server error occurred. Finally, Data? is the raw payload returned by the server; it may be nil even when there is a valid response, so never assume it is present. A robust handler checks in the order: error first, then response/status code, then data. One misconception is checking data first — this can hide transport errors or server failures. Use this disciplined order to give clear user feedback and to avoid attempting to decode absent or invalid data. Completion Handler Anatomy means check error first, then cast and check response status code, and only then process data to avoid hidden failures.. In practical terms, understanding data, response, and error parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Completion Handler Anatomy
Three parameters explained
  • Error? — Indicates network-level failures. Check first and bail when non-nil.
  • URLResponse? — Cast to HTTPURLResponse to read statusCode and headers.
  • Data? — The payload to decode. May be nil even on some responses.
Misconception: treating non-nil Data as success. Data may exist while the server returned a 500 error page. Always validate the status code.
Example check order
Check error, then guard let httpResponse = response as? HTTPURLResponse and ensure 200...299, then guard let data = data to parse.
Analogy
Think of error as the delivery truck breaking down, response as the form telling you if the package was accepted, and data as the contents of the package.
Key Takeaway

The reliable pattern is error → response → data. That order prevents misinterpreting errors as valid data.

screens.title: HTTP Status Codes and HTTPURLResponse
screens.narratorSegment: HTTP status codes tell you how the server interpreted your request. A 200-level status usually means success, 400-level codes indicate client errors such as a malformed request or missing resource, and 500-level codes are server-side failures. In Swift you retrieve status codes by casting URLResponse to HTTPURLResponse and reading its statusCode property. For example, a 404 indicates Not Found and a 500 indicates an internal server error. Your app should handle these gracefully: show a friendly message, offer retry options, or fall back to cached content. A misconception is to treat any returned data as success regardless of status. Some APIs return error pages with H T M L bodies even on 500 errors; decoding such responses as JSON will fail. Therefore check the status code before attempting to decode. In practice, treat 200–299 as success, handle 401/403 as authentication errors, and present meaningful UI feedback for transient server errors so users understand the situation. HTTP Status Codes and HTTPURLResponse means cast to httpurlresponse to read statuscode. accept 200–299 as success and handle other ranges with appropriate user feedback.. In practical terms, interpret server signals and handle non-2xx responses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Your app should handle these gracefully: show a friendly message, offer retry options, or fall back to cached content. A misconception is to treat any returned data as success regardless of status. Some APIs return error pages with H T M L bodies even on 500 errors; decoding such responses as JSON will fail. Therefore check the status code before attempting to decode. In practice, treat 200–299 as success, handle 401/403 as authentication errors, and present meaningful UI feedback for transient server errors so users understand the situation. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › HTTP Status Codes
Status ranges
  • 200–299: Success — proceed to parse data.
  • 400–499: Client errors — check request, authentication, or resource path.
  • 500–599: Server errors — usually temporary or require server-side fixes.
Handling non-2xx responses
When you receive a 4xx or 5xx status, do not attempt to decode the body as if it were valid model JSON. Instead surface a helpful message and log the status code for diagnostics. For authentication failures like 401, guide the user to re-authenticate. For 429 or 503, consider exponential backoff or displaying a retry option.
Example: 404 Not Found — show "Content not found" and avoid decoding.
Example: 500 Internal Server Error — inform the user and suggest retrying later.
Key Takeaway

Status codes are authoritative signals from the server. Use them to decide whether to parse, retry, or surface an error to the user.

screens.title: App Transport Security (ATS)
screens.narratorSegment: App Transport Security is an iOS feature that enforces secure network connections by default. Since iOS 9, ATS requires HTTPS endpoints using modern TLS. If your app tries to connect to an insecure HTTP endpoint, the system blocks that connection unless you explicitly configure an exception in Info. plist. That makes HTTPS the recommended path: it provides encrypted communication and reduces the risk of eavesdropping or tampering. A common beginner response is to add a broad exception to Info. plist to allow all HTTP traffic; this weakens security and is not recommended. Instead, if you truly must call a legacy HTTP server, add a narrowly scoped exception for that specific domain and consider migrating the server to HTTPS. In practice you will avoid ATS issues by choosing APIs that support TLS. When testing, an ATS failure often appears as a network error; use console logs and the device logs to diagnose whether a blocked connection was caused by ATS. Prioritize using HTTPS for production apps. App Transport Security (ATS) means ios blocks insecure http by default; prefer https endpoints and avoid broad info.plist exceptions.. What ATS enforces

  • Block insecure HTTP connections unless explicit exceptions exist.

Misconception: adding NSAllowsArbitraryLoads is an easy fix. It weakens app security and should be avoided for production apps.
Practical advice

Security-first: HTTPS protects your users and reduces the chance of sensitive data exposure.

screens.title: Threading and UI updates
screens.narratorSegment: Network requests are asynchronous and completed on a background queue. If you attempt to update views directly from the completion handler you risk race conditions or runtime warnings because UI work must run on the main thread. The safe pattern: perform network and decoding work in the background, then wrap any UI modifications in DispatchQueue. main. async to schedule them on the main queue. For example, after decoding posts into model objects, call DispatchQueue. main. async to assign the array to a published property or reload a table view. A common misconception is that URLSession calls the completion handler on the main queue; it does not guarantee that. Another pitfall is performing heavy decoding synchronously on the main thread — large JSON parsing can still freeze the UI. Offload C P U-heavy work to a background queue and marshal only the final UI assignment back to main. This approach keeps the app responsive and improves perceived performance for users. Threading and UI updates means run network and parsing on background queues; dispatch ui updates back to dispatchqueue.main.async to avoid freezes and warnings.. In practical terms, move data processing off the main thread and update ui safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Threading and UI updates
Recommended flow
  1. Start the network request on a background queue via URLSession.
  2. Parse or decode Data on a background queue to avoid heavy CPU work on main.
  3. Dispatch UI updates back to DispatchQueue.main.async when you set model properties or refresh views.
Common mistake: updating a published property directly inside the background handler without dispatching to main. This can produce UI glitches or runtime warnings.
Concrete code pattern
URLSession.shared.dataTask(with: url) { data, response, error in
  // parse on background
  if let data = data {
    do {
      let decoded = try JSONDecoder().decode([Post].self, from: data)
      DispatchQueue.main.async {
        self.posts = decoded // UI-safe update
      }
    } catch {
      // handle decoding error
    }
  }
}.resume()
Because decoding can be expensive, decode off the main thread and only assign the final result to UI state on the main thread.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › PostFetcher and SwiftUI
PostFetcher (excerpt)
struct Post: Codable, Identifiable {
  let userId: Int
  let id: Int
  let title: String
  let body: String
}

class PostFetcher: ObservableObject {
  @Published var posts: [Post] = []
  @Published var errorMessage: String?

  private let apiURL = URL(string: "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts")!

  func fetchPosts() {
    errorMessage = nil
    URLSession.shared.dataTask(with: apiURL) { data, response, error in
      if let error = error {
        DispatchQueue.main.async { self.errorMessage = "Network error: \(error.localizedDescription)" }
        return
      }

      guard let httpResponse = response as? HTTPURLResponse,
            (200...299).contains(httpResponse.statusCode) else {
        let statusCode = (response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode ?? -1
        DispatchQueue.main.async { self.errorMessage = "Server error: HTTP Status Code \(statusCode)" }
        return
      }

      guard let data = data else {
        DispatchQueue.main.async { self.errorMessage = "No data received from server." }
        return
      }

      do {
        let decodedPosts = try JSONDecoder().decode([Post].self, from: data)
        DispatchQueue.main.async { self.posts = decodedPosts }
      } catch {
        DispatchQueue.main.async { self.errorMessage = "Decoding error: \(error.localizedDescription)" }
      }
    }.resume()
  }
}
ContentView (excerpt)
struct ContentView: View {
  @StateObject private var postFetcher = PostFetcher()

  var body: some View {
    NavigationView {
      VStack {
        if let errorMessage = postFetcher.errorMessage {
          Text(errorMessage).foregroundColor(.red).padding()
        }

        List(postFetcher.posts) { post in
          VStack(alignment: .leading) {
            Text(post.title).font(.headline)
            Text(post.body).font(.subheadline).foregroundColor(.gray)
          }
        }
        .navigationTitle("Posts")
        .onAppear { postFetcher.fetchPosts() }
      }
    }
  }
}
This example shows the full flow: fetch, decode, and update UI safely. Use the errorMessage to present user-facing feedback for issues like network failure or decoding problems.

Logging the raw response string before decoding helps identify mismatched formats. Another frequent issue is forgetting to call resume() on the data task; the request will never run. Also confirm you are dispatching UI-updates to the main queue to avoid warnings. For transient server errors implement retry logic or backoff for resilience. Finally, present meaningful messages to users rather than raw error text, and log details for debugging during development. fullNarratorScript:
Networking is what lets your app become data-driven. In iOS the foundational A P I for HTTP work is URLSession. In this lesson you will learn how to form valid URLs, wrap them when needed in URLRequest, and use URLSession. shared. dataTask to perform GET requests. We will emphasize safe patterns: checking for network errors first, verifying HTTP status codes, and decoding data. You will also learn why App Transport Security forces HTTPS by default and how that shapes secure A P I choices. A compact Swift example will show a real GET request against a public test endpoint, and a small SwiftUI activity later will connect that fetch to a list of posts. By the end you will understand the standard completion-handler pattern and how to avoid common mistakes like blocking the main thread or assuming data is always present. Keep an eye on status codes, treat the completion handler as asynchronous, and plan to move decoding to the next step. Consider how your app should behave when the network is slow — what feedback will you show the user?

These objectives frame the practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand networking fundamentals in iOS and why URLSession is the primary A P I for HTTP work. That concept includes recognizing when to use the shared session versus a custom session. Second, you'll learn how to construct valid URL and URLRequest objects so requests don't fail at runtime. We'll show how invalid URL strings lead to nil and how to guard against crashes. Third, you'll implement a basic GET request using URLSession. shared. dataTask, observe how the completion handler returns Data, URLResponse and Error, and learn the pattern of starting the task with resume(). Fourth, you will inspect responses safely by converting URLResponse to HTTPURLResponse and checking status codes before parsing data. Each objective is paired with a simple verification milestone so you can confirm competency in a tiny hands-on step.

This second objectives slide focuses on safety and UI integration. You will practice checking for network-level errors first inside the completion handler so you don't attempt to use invalid response data. You will learn to cast the URLResponse to HTTPURLResponse to access HTTP status codes and treat only 200–299 ranges as success. You will also consider App Transport Security and why HTTPS endpoints are the recommended solution to avoid crashes. Finally, you will adopt the pattern of performing network work off the main thread and dispatching UI updates back to the main queue. These checks are small but essential; skipping them is a common source of bugs. The micro-milestones verify that you can detect a bad URL, capture a network error, report non-2xx status codes, and update a simple UI on the main thread after a successful fetch.

When we say "networking" in iOS, we mean the code path that lets an app send requests and receive responses over the internet. This includes everything from retrieving a JSON payload to downloading an image. URLSession is the native A P I that performs these tasks. Think of URLSession as the plumbing and worker threads: you hand it an address and instructions, it performs the transfer, and then it calls back with the results. A concrete example: an app fetches a list of posts to display in a feed. The app creates a URL pointing to the posts endpoint, calls URLSession. shared. dataTask, and when the server replies, the completion handler receives data or an error. A common misconception is that URLSession itself decodes responses into model objects. It does not; URLSession gives you raw Data. Decoding into Swift structs using JSONDecoder is a separate step. Another frequent confusion is assuming network calls are synchronous; they are asynchronous — you register a completion handler and resume the task. Key takeaway: URLSession executes HTTP work asynchronously and returns Data, response, and error; your job is to validate and decode safely.

Building a valid URL and, when necessary, a URLRequest are small steps that prevent runtime errors. Start by creating a URL from a well-formed string. If URL(string:) returns nil, the string is invalid and you must handle that case before continuing. For simple GETs you can pass a URL directly to dataTask; for more control—adding headers, query parameters, or using other methods—wrap the URL in a URLRequest and set its httpMethod. A practical scenario: you want to request a protected resource and must include an Authorization header. You would build a URLRequest, set the header field, and then pass that request to dataTask. A common misconception is that adding percent-encoded query parameters is optional; incorrectly encoded URLs will fail to initialize. Also avoid force-unwrapping URL objects. In short: validate the string, safely construct URL, use URLRequest when you need configuration, and never rely on implicit unwrapping. This leads to more predictable error handling and easier debugging. Constructing URLs and URLRequest means validate url strings, prefer urlrequest when you need headers or methods, and avoid force-unwrapping to prevent runtime crashes.. In practical terms, make safe addresses and request objects for get operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a concrete GET-request function to solidify the pattern. The function begins by safely creating a URL. If that fails we print an error and return. Next we create a data task using URLSession. shared. dataTask(with: url) and provide a completion handler that receives data, response, and error. Inside the handler we first check error; a non-nil error typically indicates a connectivity or transport failure. If error is nil, we cast response to HTTPURLResponse and inspect the statusCode, accepting only codes in the 200 to 299 range. If the status code indicates a server-side problem we log it and return. Finally we check that data is non-nil and then convert it to a readable string for inspection. The final step is calling resume() on the task to start it. A common mistake is forgetting resume() or performing blocking work on the main thread. This pattern guarantees you see either an error, a non-success HTTP status, or readable data. Try running this function with a valid URL and an invalid URL to observe the different code paths. Making a GET request with dataTask means create the url, call datatask, check error → cast response and check status code → unwrap data → process. always call resume().. In practical terms, complete example: error, response, and data handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Both URL and URLRequest appear in nearly every networked app. URL is simply the address of a resource. For basic GET requests where you only need to read a public endpoint, creating a URL and passing it directly to dataTask is concise and sufficient. URLRequest wraps a URL and provides configuration: the HTTP method, headers, timeout, and body. Use URLRequest when you must set an Authorization header, specify Content-Type, or switch to POST or PUT. A common beginner mistake is always wrapping with URLRequest even when unnecessary; that adds verbosity but doesn't harm functionality. Conversely, another mistake is trying to add headers by mutating a URL — headers belong to URLRequest. Example scenario: requesting a JSON feed without authentication — use URL directly. Example with authentication: build a URLRequest, set request. httpMethod = "GET", and add the Authorization header. Both are valid; choose the simpler option when possible and the configurable option when you need control. This keeps code readable and maintainable. URL vs URLRequest means use url for simple gets. use urlrequest when you need headers, custom methods, or other request configuration.. In practical terms, when to use the simple url and when to configure a request. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The completion handler of dataTask delivers three optional values: Data?, URLResponse?, and Error?. These three items represent the result of the network operation. First, Error? indicates a network-level failure such as no internet, DNS lookup failure, or a cancelled request. If error is non-nil, you should usually stop and surface a friendly message. Second, URLResponse? holds metadata about the transfer and can often be cast to HTTPURLResponse to access the HTTP status code. That status code tells you whether the request was successful (200–299) or whether a client or server error occurred. Finally, Data? is the raw payload returned by the server; it may be nil even when there is a valid response, so never assume it is present. A robust handler checks in the order: error first, then response/status code, then data. One misconception is checking data first — this can hide transport errors or server failures. Use this disciplined order to give clear user feedback and to avoid attempting to decode absent or invalid data. HTTP status codes tell you how the server interpreted your request. A 200-level status usually means success, 400-level codes indicate client errors such as a malformed request or missing resource, and 500-level codes are server-side failures. In Swift you retrieve status codes by casting URLResponse to HTTPURLResponse and reading its statusCode property. For example, a 404 indicates Not Found and a 500 indicates an internal server error. Your app should handle these gracefully: show a friendly message, offer retry options, or fall back to cached content. A misconception is to treat any returned data as success regardless of status. Some APIs return error pages with H T M L bodies even on 500 errors; decoding such responses as JSON will fail. Therefore check the status code before attempting to decode. In practice, treat 200–299 as success, handle 401/403 as authentication errors, and present meaningful UI feedback for transient server errors so users understand the situation. App Transport Security is an iOS feature that enforces secure network connections by default. Since iOS 9, ATS requires HTTPS endpoints using modern TLS. If your app tries to connect to an insecure HTTP endpoint, the system blocks that connection unless you explicitly configure an exception in Info. plist. That makes HTTPS the recommended path: it provides encrypted communication and reduces the risk of eavesdropping or tampering. A common beginner response is to add a broad exception to Info. plist to allow all HTTP traffic; this weakens security and is not recommended. Instead, if you truly must call a legacy HTTP server, add a narrowly scoped exception for that specific domain and consider migrating the server to HTTPS. In practice you will avoid ATS issues by choosing APIs that support TLS. When testing, an ATS failure often appears as a network error; use console logs and the device logs to diagnose whether a blocked connection was caused by ATS. Prioritize using HTTPS for production apps. App Transport Security (ATS) means ios blocks insecure http by default; prefer https endpoints and avoid broad info.plist exceptions.. Network requests are asynchronous and completed on a background queue. If you attempt to update views directly from the completion handler you risk race conditions or runtime warnings because UI work must run on the main thread. The safe pattern: perform network and decoding work in the background, then wrap any UI modifications in DispatchQueue. main. async to schedule them on the main queue. For example, after decoding posts into model objects, call DispatchQueue. main. async to assign the array to a published property or reload a table view. A common misconception is that URLSession calls the completion handler on the main queue; it does not guarantee that. Another pitfall is performing heavy decoding synchronously on the main thread — large JSON parsing can still freeze the UI. Offload C P U-heavy work to a background queue and marshal only the final UI assignment back to main. This approach keeps the app responsive and improves perceived performance for users. Threading and UI updates means run network and parsing on background queues; dispatch ui updates back to dispatchqueue.main.async to avoid freezes and warnings.. When network requests fail, diagnosing the cause quickly helps you fix the code. Start by confirming the URL string is valid; an invalid URL will cause URL(string:) to return nil. If the URL is valid but the request fails, check the error description — it often reveals DNS lookup failures or transport errors. If you suspect App Transport Security, try an HTTPS endpoint or review Info. plist for exceptions. When the response arrives but decoding fails, inspect the statusCode: an H T M L error page often accompanies 500 responses and will not decode as JSON. Logging the raw response string before decoding helps identify mismatched formats. Another frequent issue is forgetting to call resume() on the data task; the request will never run. Also confirm you are dispatching UI-updates to the main queue to avoid warnings. For transient server errors implement retry logic or backoff for resilience. Finally, present meaningful messages to users rather than raw error text, and log details for debugging during development. Keep a short list of practical rules next time you implement networking. First, always validate your URL and avoid force-unwrapping. Second, follow the handler order: check error, then response and status code, then data. Third, use URLRequest when you need headers or different methods, otherwise a URL is sufficient for simple GETs. Fourth, respect App Transport Security and prefer HTTPS; only add narrow exceptions as a last resort. Fifth, do network and parsing work off the main thread and marshal UI updates back to the main queue. These rules reduce crashes, make debugging simpler, and produce a responsive user experience.
